title: FiuLa - Prospective Pedobarographic Interventional Study on the Biomechanical Efficacy of a Standardized Felt Offloading Technique in People with Diabetic Foot Syndrome and Healthy Participants (Felt Under Load)
summary: In people with diabetes, reduced sensation in the feet can lead to pressure areas and wounds or cause them to recur. Felt padding is used to redistribute pressure during walking from heavily loaded areas of the foot to other areas. This study investigates how effectively felt padding applied according to a standardized procedure reduces pressure under the foot and whether this effect remains after a few days. People with diabetes who have had pressure areas or foot wounds in the past, as well as healthy volunteers, may take part. Pressure under the foot is measured during walking before and after the padding is applied and again after two to four days, using thin measuring insoles placed inside the shoes; in addition, the number of steps taken in everyday life is recorded. Participants are also asked about wearing comfort, any pain, and their experience while walking.

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
Patients with diabetic foot syndrome
- Type 1, type 2, or type 3 diabetes mellitus
- Aged 18 to 85 years
- Clinically confirmed polyneuropathy
- History of a pressure ulcer or pre-ulcerative lesion beneath a metatarsal head (MTH 1, MTH 2/3, or MTH 4/5)
-Willingness to wear the pedometer continuously

Healthy participants
-Aged 18 to 85 years
-No known diabetic foot syndrome
-Willingness to wear the pedometer continuously
Exclusion criteria:
Patients with diabetic foot syndrome
- Plantar loading conditions that do not permit standardized offloading for MTH 1, MTH 2/3, or MTH 4/5, including severe deformities or previous amputations, as determined by the investigator
- Previous offloading surgery in the affected area
- Gait instability that prevents safe ascent and descent of one flight of stairs
- Active ulcer on the side being examined
-Severe somatic comorbidity that, in the investigator’s judgement, makes participation inappropriate
-Severe psychiatric disorder associated with impaired capacity to provide informed consent or to cooperate with study procedures, as determined by the investigator
-Pregnancy
-Active Charcot foot

Healthy participants
-Known or clinically confirmed diabetic foot syndrome
-Severe comorbidity
-Severe psychiatric disorder
-Pregnancy
